rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi prefers that disbelievers alone are questioned: Hasan says only Hell's people are asked, and the report about Abu Bakr's shared meal is answered that such questioning concerns disbelievers.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن : لا يسأل عن النعيم إلا أهل النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers' pursuit of worldly abundance and its pleasures distracted them from obedience and gratitude, so questioning will expose that their supposed happiness caused their afterlife misery.
rows.anchor: ألهاهم التكاثر بالدنيا والتفاخر بلذاتها عن طاعة الله تعالى والاشتغال بشكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second view extends questioning to believers and disbelievers, supported by reports about bodily health, cold water, food, shelter, and other ordinary comforts.
rows.anchor: والقول الثاني : أنه عام في حق المؤمن والكافر واحتجوا بأحاديث

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Prophet says the first question concerns blessing, asking whether a servant's body was made sound and he was given cold water.
rows.anchor: روى أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال : ( أول ما يسأل عنه العبد

rows.speaker: محمود بن لبيد
rows.claim: When companions asked what blessing they could be questioned about amid hardship, the Prophet replied that such questioning would come later.
rows.anchor: وقال محمود بن لبيد : لما نزلت هذه السورة قالوا : يا رسول الله عن أبي نعيم : نسأل

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Umar asks what blessing could be questioned when they had been driven from homes and wealth; the Prophet names shade, shelter, and cold water.
rows.anchor: وروى عن عمر أنه قال : أي نعيم نسأل عنه يا رسول الله وقد أخرجنا من ديارنا وأموالنا ؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A related prophetic report describes a person safe at home, healthy, and possessing a day's food as if the whole world had been given to him.
rows.anchor: من أصبح آمنا في سربه معافى في بدنه وعنده قوت يومه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A newly converted young man declines a richly furnished marriage after recalling the warning, saying he cannot bear to answer for such luxury.
rows.anchor: فعلمه رسول الله سورة ألهاكم ثم زوجه رسول الله امرأة فلما دخل عليها

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: When a needy man asks whether he has any blessing, the Prophet answers that shade, sandals, and cold water count.
rows.anchor: وعن أنس لما نزلت الآية قام محتاج فقال : هل علي من النعمة شيء ؟

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Hungry, the Prophet, Abu Bakr, and Umar visit Abu al-Haytham; after eating bread, meat, dates, and drinking water, the Prophet identifies the meal as a blessing to be questioned about.
rows.anchor: فأكلوا وشربوا فقال عليه الصلاة والسلام : ( هذا من النعيم الذي تسألون عنه )

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A prophetic report says a servant's feet will not move until he is asked about four matters: lifespan, wealth, youth, and deeds.
rows.anchor: لا تزول قدما عبد حتى يسأل عن أربع عن عمره وماله وشبابه وعمله

rows.speaker: معاذ
rows.claim: Muadh transmits that questioning reaches even an eye's kohl, a crumb of clay on one's finger, and touching a brother's garment.
rows.anchor: وعن معاذ عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم : ( أن العبد ليسأل يوم القيامة حتى عن كحل عينيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi concludes questioning includes both believers and disbelievers: for disbelievers it is rebuke for ingratitude, while for grateful, obedient believers it is an honor.
rows.anchor: السؤال يعم المؤمن والكافر ، لكن سؤال الكافر توبيخ لأنه ترك الشكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report identifies five blessings: a full stomach, cool drink, pleasure of sleep, shaded dwellings, and balanced temperament.
rows.anchor: ما روى أنه خمس : شبع / البطون وبارد الشراب ولذة النوم وإظلال المساكن

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud identifies the questioned blessings as security, health, and free time.
rows.anchor: قال ابن مسعود : إنه الأمن والصحة والفراغ

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas takes the blessings to mean health and all pleasures of food and drink.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : إنه الصحة وسائر ملاذ المأكول والمشروب

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another view says people are questioned about using the faculties of hearing and sight.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم : الانتفاع بإدراك السمع والبصر

rows.speaker: الحسن بن الفضل
rows.claim: Hasan ibn al-Fadl identifies the blessings as eased religious obligations and the Quran's facilitation.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن بن الفضل : تخفيف الشرائع وتيسير القرآن

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn Umar singles out cold water, which Razi later treats as one example within the larger category of blessings.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عمر : إنه الماء البارد

rows.speaker: الباقر
rows.claim: Al-Baqir says the blessing is the well-being God gives; in a report to Jabir al-Ju'fi, he says the Prophet himself is the great blessing who rescued people from error.
rows.anchor: قال : النعيم هو رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنعم الله به على هذا العالم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some restrict the question to surplus beyond necessary food, clothing, and lodging.
rows.anchor: إنما يسألون عن الزائد مما لا بد منه من مطعم وملبس ومسكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi prefers all blessings: the definite article is comprehensive, no evidence favors excluding some, the same wording covers all gifts to Israel, and complete blessing is an integrated whole.
rows.anchor: والتاسع : وهو الأولى أنه يجب حمله على جميع النعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Blessings divide into outward and inward, connected and separate, religious and worldly; they cannot be enumerated by type and individual instance.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن النعم أقسام فمنها ظاهرة وباطنة ، ومنها متصلة ومنفصلة ، ومنها دينية ودنيوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi ironically directs readers to doctors, astrologers, and kings to recognize bodily, cosmic, and political gifts, noting these specialists are especially heedless or ignorant of their source.
rows.anchor: استعن في معرفة نعم الله عليك في صحة بدنك بالأطباء ، ثم هم أشد الخلق غفلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Umar's mention of cold water means one blessing among many; it is singled out as cheap yet desperately missed, illustrated by Ibn al-Sammak asking Harun al-Rashid whether he would trade half a kingdom for water in a desert.
rows.anchor: وأما الذي يروى عن ابن عمر أنه الماء البارد فمعناه هذا من جملته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Water may be singled out because Hell's inhabitants crave it more intensely than anything else.
rows.anchor: أو لأن أهل النار يطلبون الماء أشد من طلبهم لغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation for mentioning cold water and shade is that the surah addresses affluent people who particularly enjoy them.
rows.anchor: أو لأن السورة نزلت في المترفين ، وهم المختصون بالماء البارد والظل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question covers every blessing, necessary or surplus, for both believers and disbelievers, since every gift should be spent in God's obedience; the four-question report includes all gifts.
rows.anchor: والحق أن السؤال يعم المؤمن والكافر عن جميع النعيم سواء كان مما لا بد منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view places the questioning at the accounting station; Razi answers the apparent sequence by reading then as a later statement about the Day of Resurrection, as in the cited passage.
rows.anchor: فالقول الأول : أن هذا السؤال إنما يكون في موقف الحساب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second view places questioning after entry into Hell, when its keepers question the condemned and ask what led them to Saqar; the Prophet's coming was itself a blessing for which they are questioned.
rows.anchor: القول الثاني : أنهم إذا دخلوا النار سئلوا عن النعيم توبيخا لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi suggests angels may tell the damned that their worldly indulgence distracted them from saving deeds, so they would have been saved had they spent life obeying God.
rows.anchor: اشتغلتم بالنعيم عن العمل الذي ينجيكم من هذه النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wail is a word of blame and wrath, a cry uttered by the distressed; its original form is separated from the following word, then convention joined it to the lām.
rows.anchor: الويل لفظة الذم والسخط ، وهي كلمة كل مكروب يتولون فيدعو بالويل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report identifies Wail as a mountain in Hell; Razi explains its indefiniteness as signaling a reality whose full nature only God knows.
rows.anchor: وروى أنه جبل في جهنم إن قيل : لم قال : ههنا :

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another lexical distinction makes wail a term of condemnation, wais belittlement, and wayh compassion, marking the act as vile.
rows.anchor: وقيل : في ويل إنها كلمة تقبيح ، وويس استصغار وويح ترحم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning is general for anyone who acts this way, since a specific occasion does not restrict general wording.
rows.anchor: أما المحققون فقالوا : إنه عام لكل من يفعل هذا الفعل كائنا من كان

rows.speaker: عطاء والكلبي
rows.claim: Ataa and al-Kalbi say the surah was revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, who slandered people, especially the Messenger.
rows.anchor: ثم قال عطاى والكلبي : نزلت في الأخنس بن شريق كان يلمز الناس

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil identifies al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who backbit the Prophet behind his back and attacked him to his face.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل : نزلت في الوليد بن المغيرة كان يغتاب النبي

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq says they had long heard that the surah was revealed about Umayya ibn Khalaf.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن إسحاق : ما زلنا نسمع أن هذه السورة نزلت في أمية بن خلف

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says general wording can still refer to one person, as ordinary speech may use a universal statement while intending a familiar individual.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : وكون اللفظ عاما لا ينافي أن يكون المراد منه شخصا معينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamz means breaking and lamz means stabbing or attacking; here the image is damaging people's reputations and belittling them.
rows.anchor: الهمز الكسر قال تعالى : { هماز مشاء } واللمز الطعن والمراد الكسر من أعراض الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading with a still mīm in both words denotes a mocker who performs oddities and jokes, provoking laughter and abuse.
rows.anchor: وقرىء : { ويل لكل همزة لمزة } بسكون الميم وهي المسخرة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses hamaza as backbiter and lamaza as fault-finder.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : الهمزة المغتاب ، واللمزة العياب

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abu Zayd distinguishes hamz by hand from lamz by tongue.
rows.anchor: قال أبو زيد : الهمزة باليد واللمزة / باللسان

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abu al-Aliya distinguishes face-to-face taunting from fault-finding behind someone's back.
rows.anchor: قال أبو العالية : الهمزة بالمواجهة واللمزة بظهر الغيب

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says the hamza breaks a companion's spirit with a contemptuous look, while the lamza speaks ill of and faults a brother.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن : الهمزة الذي يهمز جليسه يكسر عليه عينه

rows.speaker: أبو الجوزاء
rows.claim: Abu al-Jawza asks Ibn Abbas who is condemned; Ibn Abbas answers that they spread tales, divide friends, and label people with faults.
rows.anchor: عن أبي الجوزاء قال : قلت لابن عباس : { ويل لكل همزة لمزة } من هؤلاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All definitions converge on attacking and exposing faults, whether seriously from envy or hatred or jokingly to amuse; the offense may target religious appearance or conduct, speech, or gesture, in a person's presence or absence.
rows.anchor: جميع هذه الوجوه متقاربة راجعة إلى أصل واحد وهو الطعن وإظهار العيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every form is prohibited, explicitly where the word applies and by clear analogy otherwise; attacking the Prophet is especially grave because of his supreme religious station.
rows.anchor: وكل ذلك داخل تحت النهي والزجر ، إنما البحث في أن اللفظ بحسب اللغة موضوع لماذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Akhladahu and khalladahu have the same meaning.
rows.anchor: أخلده وخلده بمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation is that wealth prolongs a person's hopes until he imagines it has made him immortal; the past tense portrays survival as a guarantee already settled.
rows.anchor: يحسب هذا الإنسان أن المال ضمن له الخلود وأعطاه الأمان من الموت

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan remarks that death is the certain reality most like a doubt to which people give no credence.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن : ما رأيت يقينا لا شك فيه أشبه بشك لا يقين فيه كالموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second interpretation is that he builds sturdy structures as someone expecting a long life or hoping to be remembered after death.
rows.anchor: يعمل الأعمال المحكمة كتشييد البنيان بالآجر والجص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation is an extreme love of wealth: the miser imagines losing any of it would mean dying, so he hoards to preserve life.
rows.anchor: ثالثها : أحب المال حبا شديدا حتى اعتقد أنه : إن انتقص مالي أموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth interpretation alludes to righteous deeds, which preserve a person's good name in this world and bring enduring bliss in the next.
rows.anchor: أن هذا تعريض بالعمل الصالح وأنه هو الذي يخلد صاحبه في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kalla may rebuke the belief that money grants immortality, since knowledge and righteousness endure; Ali contrasts dead hoarders with living scholars.
rows.anchor: ليس الأمر كما يظن أن المال يخلده بل العلم والصلاح

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali says wealth keepers die while scholars remain as long as time endures.
rows.anchor: مات خزان المال وهم أحياء والعلماء باقون ما بقي الدهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, kalla means truly; the lām of yunbadh answers an implied oath and conveys certainty.
rows.anchor: والقول الثاني معناه حقا : { لينبذن } واللام في : { لينبذن } جواب القسم المقدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yunbadh, 'he will be cast away,' conveys humiliation because the disbeliever believed himself honored.
rows.anchor: فإنما ذكره بلفظ النبذ الدال على الإهانة ، لأن الكافر كان يعتقد أنه من أهل الكرامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading says 'we shall cast him and his wealth away'; another, with a ḍamma on the dhāl, includes him and his supporters.
rows.anchor: وقرىء لنبذان أي هو وماله ولينبذن بضم الذال أي هو وأنصاره

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad explains Hutama as a fire that crushes whoever enters it; the root means breaking, and a harsh shepherd is called a crusher of livestock.
rows.anchor: وأما : { الحطمة } فقال المبرد : إنها النار التي تحطم كل من وقع / فيها ورجل حطمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators call Hutama a name for Hell and its second level; Muqatil says it crushes bones, consumes flesh, and reaches hearts.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون : الحطمة اسم من أسماء النار وهي الدركة الثانية من دركات النار

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A prophetic report says an angel breaks the disbeliever across the spine as a stick is snapped over a knee, then throws him into the fire.
rows.anchor: روى عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال : ( إن الملك ليأخذ الكافر فيكسره على صلبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hutama aptly answers the slanderer's breakage of another's standing: the Fire breaks him completely and casts him into Hell's depths.
rows.anchor: الهامز بكسر عين ليضع قدره فيلقيه في الحضيض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name also mirrors the slanderer's consumption of people's flesh, since this fire consumes skin and flesh.
rows.anchor: الهماز اللماز يأكل لحم الناس والحطمة أيضا اسم للنار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One name for Hell answers the two offenses of hamz and lamz; the response to how one name suffices is that the hearer does not know this formidable Hutama.
rows.anchor: ويمكن أن يقال : ذكر وصفين الهمز واللمز ، ثم قابلهما باسم واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The genitive 'Allah's Fire' magnifies it as unlike ordinary fires; al-muqada means either eternally burning or kindled by God's command or power.
rows.anchor: الإضافة للتفخيم أي هي نار لا كسائر النيران

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali marvels at anyone disobeying God while fire blazes beneath the earth.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول علي عليه السلام : عجبا ممن يعصى الله على وجه الأرض والنار تسعر من تحته

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says Hell was kindled for a thousand years until red, another thousand until white, and another until black; it is now dark and black.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث : ( أوقد عليها ألف سنة حتى احمرت ، ثم ألف سنة حتى ابيضت ، ثم ألف سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb tala'a/ittala'a can mean climbing onto or ascending over a mountain.
rows.anchor: فاعلم أنه يقال : طلع الجبل واطلع عليه إذا علاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation is that fire enters the body up to the chest and heart, the body's most delicate and pain-sensitive part; it does not consume the heart fully, or the sufferers would die.
rows.anchor: النار تدخل في أجوافهم حتى تصل إلى صدورهم وتطلع على أفئدتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second interpretation singles out hearts because they house disbelief, corrupt beliefs, and wicked intentions.
rows.anchor: سبب تخصيص الأفئدة بذلك هو أنها مواطن الكفر والعقائد الخبيثة

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to say the Fire consumes its inhabitants until it reaches their hearts and stops; God then restores their flesh and bones.
rows.anchor: روى عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أن النار تأكل أهلها حتى إذا اطلعت على أفئدتهم انتهت

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan glosses mu'sada as shut or closed; isdad and isad are two dialectal forms.
rows.anchor: فقال الحسن : { مؤصدة } أي مطبقة من أصدت الباب / وأوصدته لغتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word evokes closed doors; saying only 'covered' would miss the door's meaning.
rows.anchor: ولم يقل : مطبقة لأن المؤصدة هي الأبواب المغلقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment is intensified by casting them into a deep-bottomed place like a well.
rows.anchor: أن قوله : { لينبذن } يقتضي أنه موضع له قعر عميق جدا كالبئر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sealing the doors makes them remember the possibility of escape, increasing their anguish.
rows.anchor: لكنه بالباب يذكرهم الخروج ، فيزيد في حسرتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Placing 'upon them' before 'sealed' foregrounds their trapped condition as the primary point.
rows.anchor: وثالثها : أنه قال : { عليهم مؤصدة } ولم يقل : مؤصدة عليهم لأن قوله : { عليهم مؤصدة }

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: The readings include ʿumud with two ḍammas, ʿamad with a still mīm, and ʿamad with two fatḥas; al-Farra compares other words with the same patterns.
rows.anchor: المسألة الأولى : قرىء في عمد بضمتين وعمد بسكون الميم وعمد بفتحتين ، قال الفراء :

rows.speaker: المبرد وأبو علي
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad and Abu Ali distinguish ʿamad as a plural of ʿamud by a nonstandard pattern from ʿamad as its regular plural, like zabur/zubur and rasul/rasul.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد وأبو علي : العمد جمع عمود على غير واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A column is any long piece of wood or iron and is a structural support, such as the pole that holds up a tent.
rows.anchor: المسألة الثانية : العمود كل مستطيل من خشب أو حديد ، وهو أصل للبناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation has columns bolting the doors shut; fī functions like bi, and their abundance makes them seem built into the door itself.
rows.anchor: أنها عمد أغلقت بها تلك الأبواب كنحو ما تغلق به الدروب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the doors seal over prisoners bound in long columns, like stocks used to restrain thieves.
rows.anchor: والقول الثاني : أن يكون المعنى : { إنها عليهم مؤصدة } حال كونهم موثقين : { فى عمد }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraha al-Ashram, Yemen's ruler under the Negus, built al-Qullays in Sana'a to divert pilgrimage to it; one report says a man from Kinana defiled it at night, another that travelers' fire burned it, prompting his vow to demolish the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: روى أن أبرهة بن الصباح الأشرم ملك اليمن من قبل أصخمة النجاشي بنى كنيسة بصنعاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraha marched with Mahmud, a powerful elephant, and eight, twelve, or a thousand other elephants according to differing reports.
rows.anchor: ومعه فيل اسمه محمود وكان قويا عظيما ، وثمانية أخرى ، وقيل : إثنا عشر ، وقيل : ألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abd al-Muttalib offered a third of Tihama's wealth to make Abraha withdraw, but he refused; the elephant knelt whenever directed toward the sanctuary and ran in other directions.
rows.anchor: خرج إليه عبد المطلب وعرض عليه ثلث أموال تهامة ليرجع فأبى

rows.speaker: عبد المطلب
rows.claim: After Abraha seized two hundred of his camels, Abd al-Muttalib said he owned the camels while the House had a Lord who would protect it.
rows.anchor: قال أنا رب الإبل وللبيت رب سيمنعك عنه

rows.speaker: عبد المطلب
rows.claim: Abd al-Muttalib prayed while holding the Kaaba's ring, asking God to protect His sanctuary and its people from the invaders.
rows.anchor: وأتى البيت وأخذ بحلقته وهو يقول :

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Strange birds arrived from Yemen, each carrying one stone in its beak and two on its legs; Ibn Abbas saw a heap at Umm Hani's house marked red like agate.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أنه رأى منها عند أم هانيء نحو قفيز مخططة بحمرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each inscribed stone struck its intended person, entering the head and exiting below; the army died along roads and watering places, while Abraha's fingers fell away and his chest split before he died.
rows.anchor: فكان الحجر يقع على رأس الرجل فيخرج من دبره ، وعلى كل حجر اسم من يقع عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraha's minister Abu Yaksum escaped, but a bird followed him to the Negus, where a stone struck and killed him as he finished his account.
rows.anchor: وانفلت وزيره أبو يكسوم وطائر يحلق فوقه ، حتى بلغ النجاشي

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha says she saw the elephant's guide and keeper later blind, lame, and begging.
rows.anchor: وعن عائشة قالت : ( رأيت قائد الفيل ) وسائسه أعميين مقعدين يستطعمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeing means knowing and recollecting: the event was so widely transmitted that its knowledge was as clear as sight; perceived events can be described as seen, unlike what is intrinsically imperceptible.
rows.anchor: المراد من الرؤية العلم والتذكير ، وهو إشارة إلى أن الخبر به متواتر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording asks how God acted rather than what He did because the manner of an event reveals the evidence of divine power and merits praise; the elephant episode showed power, knowledge, wisdom, and Muhammad's honor.
rows.anchor: هذه الكيفية هي التي يسميها المتكلمون وجه الدليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi's theology allows miracles before prophethood as preparation for and heralds of it, including the report that a cloud shaded Muhammad.
rows.anchor: مذهبنا أنه يجوز تقديم المعجزات على زمان البعثة تأسيسا لنبوتهم وإرهاصا لها

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: Mu'tazilites reject pre-prophethood miracles and therefore posit a contemporary prophet or preacher such as Khalid ibn Sinan or Quss ibn Sa'ida, perhaps sent to a small community.
rows.anchor: وعند المعتزلة ، أن ذلك لا يجوز ، فلا جرم زعموا أنه لا بد وأن يقال : كان في ذلك الزمان نبي ( أو خطيب ) كخالد بن سنان أو قس بن ساعدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The targeted birds and stones make the event a strong answer to materialists' weak naturalistic explanations of other divine punishments; many eyewitnesses remained in Mecca when the Prophet recited it, and their silence against him supports its reliable transmission.
rows.anchor: ولو كان النقل ضعيفا لشافهوه بالتكذيب ، فلما لم يكن كذلك علمنا أنه لا سبب للطعن فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿala is preferable to khalaqa, jaʿala, or ʿamila: creation marks origination, making marks qualities, and doing follows effort, whereas faʿala broadly covers all the acts in the episode.
rows.anchor: وفعل عام فكان أولى لأنه تعالى خلق الطيور وجعل طبع الفيل على خلاف ما كانت عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God 'your Lord' may distinguish Muhammad, who responds with gratitude and obedience, from those who witnessed the punishment yet kept worshipping idols.
rows.anchor: كأنه تعالى قال : إنهم لما شاهدوا هذا الانتقام ثم لم يتركوا عبادة الأوثان ، وأنت يا محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, God defeated the elephant army to honor Muhammad's coming, nurturing him before his people and promising future victory.
rows.anchor: إنما فعلت بأصحاب الفيل ذلك تعظيما لك وتشريفا لمقدمك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The event is astonishing because the Kaaba is subordinate to Muhammad: the learned Prophet is the jewel and the mosque its setting, so an army punished for attacking the sanctuary would also be destroyed for attacking him.
rows.anchor: العلم يؤدي بدون المسجد أما لا مسجد بدون العالم فالعالم هو الدر والمسجد هو الصدف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Kaaba is the qibla of prayer and the heart the qibla of knowledge; having protected the outward direction, one should preserve the religious heart from sins.
rows.anchor: ثانيها : أن الكعبة قبلة صلاتك وقلبك قبلة معرفتك ، ثم أنا حفظت قبلة عملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A companion is normally the lower party accompanying a higher one, so 'companions of the elephant' casts the people as less than the beast; it turned away from the sanctuary rather than disobey God, unlike them.
rows.anchor: فقوله : { أصحاب * الفيل } يدل على أن أولئك الأقوام كانوا أقل حال وأدون منزلة من الفيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi answers why God punished the Kaaba's attackers but not Quraysh's idol placement: idols violated God's right, while destroying the building violated human rights; public harm warrants punishment even for Muslims, whereas harmless noncombatants may be spared despite unbelief.
rows.anchor: لأن وضع الأوثان فيها تعد على حق الله تعالى ، وتخريبها تعد على حق الخلق

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj parses kayfa as accusative with faʿala, not with ألم تر, because kayfa is an interrogative word.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : كيف في موضع نصب بفعل لا بقوله : { ألم تر }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kayda means a covert intention to harm; though Abraha openly announced destruction, he secretly envied the Arabs and sought to transfer the Kaaba's prestige to himself and his city.
rows.anchor: لأنه كان يضمر الحسد للعرب ، وكان يريد صرف الشرف الحاصل لهم بسبب الكعبة

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: Mu'tazilites argue that attributing the plot to them proves God disapproves of evil, since approved evil would be attributed to Him.
rows.anchor: إضافة الكيد إليهم دليل على أنه تعالى لا يرضى بالقبيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi counters that Arabic attribution needs only a slight causal link: the plot happened in accord with the plotters' will and choice.
rows.anchor: يكفي في حسن هذه الإضافة وقوعه مطابقا لإرادتهم واختيارهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fī tadlīl means rendered futile and wasted; the church plot failed when the church burned, and the later plan to demolish the Kaaba failed through the birds; fī describes their plainly mistaken course.
rows.anchor: ونظيره قوله تعالى : { وما دعاء الكافرين إلا فى ضلال }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite tayran may belittle the birds so that God's work is more astonishing, or magnify them as remarkable birds whose tiny stones never miss.
rows.anchor: إما للتحقير فإنه مهما كان أحقر كان صنع الله أعجب وأكبر

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda defines ababil as scattered groups arriving from different directions.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة : أبابيل جماعة في تفرقة ، يقال : جاءت الخيل أبابيل أبابيل من ههنا وههنا

rows.speaker: الأخفش والفراء
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash and al-Farra say ababil has no singular, like shamāṭīt and ʿabādīd.
rows.anchor: وهو قول الأخفش والفراء : أنه لا واحد لها وهو مثل الشماطيط والعباديد

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر الرؤاسي
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar al-Ruʾasi says he heard the singular ibala, a large bundle, as in the proverb about adding a twig to a bundle.
rows.anchor: زعم أبو جعفر الرؤاسي وكان ثقة مأمونا أنه سمع واحدها إبالة

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisa'i says grammarians used ibul and ababil, by analogy with ʿajul and ʿajājīl.
rows.anchor: قال الكسائي : كنت أسمع النحويين يقولون : إبول وأبابيل كعجول وعجاجيل

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra also accepts ibāla as a singular for ababil, like dinar and dananir.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : ولو قال قائل : واحد الأبابيل إيبالة كان صوابا

rows.speaker: ابن سيرين عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Sirin transmits Ibn Abbas's description of birds with elephant-like beaks and dog-paw-like feet.
rows.anchor: روى ابن سيرين عن ابن عباس قال : كانت طيرا لها خراطيم كخراطيم الفيل

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ata transmits Ibn Abbas's report of black birds arriving from the sea in successive flocks; Razi suggests their color may mirror the people's outward and inward darkness.
rows.anchor: وروى عطاء عنه قال : طير سود جاءت من قبل البحر فوجا فوجا

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr says the birds were small and white, perhaps because white defeated the darkness of disbelief.
rows.anchor: وعن سعيد بن جبير أنها بيض صغار ولعل السبب أن ظلمة الكفر انهزمت بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other descriptions say green birds with predatory heads or mottled birds like swallows; Razi suggests separate flocks may have had different forms, and each observer described what he saw.
rows.anchor: وأقول : إنها لما كانت أفواجا ، فلعل كل فوج منها كان على شكل آخر

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة
rows.claim: Abu Haywa reads yarmihim, with God or the birds as its masculine subject; the collective noun is treated as masculine despite taking feminine agreement by sense.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو حيوة : يرميهم أي الله أو الطير لأنه اسم جمع مذكر

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says each bird carried three stones, one in its beak and two on its feet; each killed one person, bore the victim's name, and pierced through the body.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل : كان كل طائر يحمل ثلاثة أحجار ، واحد في منقاره واثنان في رجليه

rows.speaker: عكرمة عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ikrima transmits from Ibn Abbas that each stone caused a skin eruption and smallpox; Sa'id ibn Jubayr agrees, and stones ranged from lentil-sized to chickpea-sized.
rows.anchor: روى عكرمة عن ابن عباس ، قال : لما أرسل الله الحجارة على أصحاب الفيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some reject the account, arguing that a tiny stone could not pierce a person's body without undermining confidence in ordinary observation of weight and sight.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن من الناس من أنكر ذلك ، وقال : لو جوزناأن يكون في الحجارة التي تكون مثل العدسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi answers that such extraordinary events are possible on his theological view even though ordinary custom does not produce them.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن ذلك جائز على مذهبنا إلا أن العادة جارية بأنها لا تقع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation makes sijjil the name of the register recording punishment, like sijjin for the deeds register; it derives from sending, and the punishment is described as sent in related passages.
rows.anchor: أن السجيل كأنه علم للديوان الذي كتب فيه عذاب الكفار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses sijjil as a compound meaning stone and clay.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : سجيل معناه سنك وكل ، يعني بعضه حجر وبعضه طين

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda says sijjil means severe or hard.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة : السجيل الشديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations call sijjil the lowest heaven or stones from Hell, where Sijil is a name of Hell and the nūn becomes lām.
rows.anchor: ورابعها : السجيل اسم لسماء الدنيا وخامسها : السجيل حجارة من جهنم

none: verse heading and brief introduction only; explanation continues in the next segment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asf has several meanings: post-harvest leaves left in the field and eaten by livestock, straw dispersed from grain by wind, plant tips before grain matures, or kernels eaten leaving husks.
rows.anchor: وذكروا ههنا وجوها : أحدها : أنه ورق الزرع الذي يبقى في الأرض بعد الحصاد

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim specifically takes asf as straw, which wind separates from grain when winnowing; once eaten, it is spent and powerless.
rows.anchor: قال أبو مسلم : العصف التبن لقوله : { ذو العصف والريحان }

rows.speaker: مقاتل وقتادة وعطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: If ma'kul means eaten, one reading compares them to fodder digested and excreted by livestock, whose dried fragments disperse, like the army's dismembered bodies; this is attributed to Muqatil, Qatada, and Ata from Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: وهو قول مقاتل ، وقتادة وعطاء عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading of eaten fodder compares the army to crop leaves damaged by worms.
rows.anchor: أن يكون التشبيه واقعا بورق الزرع إذا وقع فيه الأكال

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan interprets the image as straw whose grain has been eaten, with 'eaten' grammatically attributed to the whole stalk because its meaning is understood.
rows.anchor: وهذا / قول الحسن

rows.speaker: عكرمة والضحاك
rows.claim: Ikrima and al-Dahhak take ma'kul as edible fodder: the army became like straw fit for animals to eat.
rows.anchor: وهو قول عكرمة والضحاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some object that al-Hajjaj destroyed the Kaaba without a similar event and infer that the Elephant story was different or had another cause; Razi replies that the earlier event was a harbinger before Muhammad's mission, when such a sign was needed.
rows.anchor: أنا بينا أن ذلك وقع إرهاصا لأمر محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

none: surah heading and verse text only

rows.speaker: الزجاج وأبو عبيدة
rows.claim: One analysis links the lām to the preceding surah: God made the army like eaten straw to preserve Quraysh and their customary winter and summer journeys.
rows.anchor: الأول : وهو قول الزجاج وأبي عبيدة أن التقدير : { فجعلهم كعصف مأكول } لإلف قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi rejects the objection that the army was destroyed only for disbelief: final recompense is deferred, and universal punishment would have affected all disbelievers, so the event also honored Quraysh.
rows.anchor: قلنا هذا السؤال ضعيف لوجوه أحدها : أنا لا نسلم أن الله تعالى إنما فعل بهم ذلك لكفرهم ، فإن الجزاء على الكفر مؤخر للقيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if rebuking unbelief was one purpose, it can coexist with the further purpose of protecting Quraysh's trade; an outcome can also be described by its eventual benefit.
rows.anchor: هب أن زجرهم عن الكفر مقصود لكن لا ينافي كون شيء آخر مقصود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second analysis attaches the lām to the prior account as a whole: God did all He did to preserve Quraysh's customary journeys.
rows.anchor: الاحتمال الثاني : أن يكون التقدير : { ألم تر كيف فعل ربك بأصحاب الفيل لإيلاف قريش }

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: A third analysis gives the lām the sense 'toward': the prior events led to another favor, namely Quraysh's accustomed journeys.
rows.anchor: / الاحتمال الثالث : أن تكون اللام في قوله : { لإيلاف } بمعنى إلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some treat the two surahs as one because the opening depends on the preceding surah, Ubayy's codex joined them, and Umar recited al-Tin and then both surahs together in Maghrib without a basmala between them.
rows.anchor: أن جعلوا السورتين سورة واحدة واحتجوا عليه بوجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The established view keeps them separate: the Quran is interconnected throughout, Ubayy's codex is outweighed by the community's consistent separation, and Umar could simply have recited two surahs together.
rows.anchor: وهو المشهور المستفيض أن هذه السورة منفصلة عن سورة الفيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mecca lacked crops and livestock, so its leading families traded in the two seasons to provide food and clothing; neighboring kings honored them as custodians and residents of God's sanctuary.
rows.anchor: فكان أشراف أهل مكة يرتحلون للتجارة هاتين الرحتلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Had the Abyssinians destroyed the Kaaba, Quraysh would have lost honor and protection and become vulnerable; their defeat instead increased their prestige and commercial benefits.
rows.anchor: فلما أهلك الله أصحاب الفيل ورد كيدهم في نحرهم ازداد وقع أهل مكة في القلوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final command to worship the Lord of this House points back to the Elephant account: God protected the Kaaba for Quraysh's benefit, making worship a fitting response to that benefit.
rows.anchor: أن قوله تعالى في آخر هذه السورة : { فليعبدوا رب هاذا البيت * الذى } إشارة إلى أول سورة الفيل

rows.speaker: الخليل وسيبويه
rows.claim: A second analysis attaches the lām to 'let them worship': Quraysh should worship the Lord of the House in gratitude and recognition of this blessing.
rows.anchor: القول الثاني : وهو أن اللام في : { لإيلاف } متعلقة بقوله : { فليعبدوا } وهو قول الخليل وسيبويه والتقدير : فليعبدوا رب هذا البيت ، لإيلاف قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ introduces the conditional sense: if they will not worship God for all His countless favors, let them at least worship Him for this manifest one.
rows.anchor: قلنا : لما في الكلام من معنى الشرط ، وذلك لأن نعم الله عليهم لا تحصى

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: A third analysis treats the lām as an exclamatory particle: marvel that Quraysh persist in error and idol worship while God unites them, averts harm, and orders their livelihood; al-Zajjaj reports this choice of al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash, and al-Farra.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : قال قوم : هذه اللام لام التعجب ، كأن المعنى : اعجبوا لإيلاف قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One meaning of ilaf is familiarity or attachment; Abu Jaʿfar reads liʾilfi, while other readers use liʾilafi and ʿIkrima reads liyafi.
rows.anchor: ألفت الشيء وألفته إلفا وإلافا وإيلافا بمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Another meaning makes ilaf God's preparation of Quraysh's attachment to the journeys, comparable to God's uniting people's hearts; the source may be understood as the object of God's action.
rows.anchor: والمعنى أن هذه الألفة إنما حصلت في قريش بتدبير الله وهو كقوله : { ولاكن الله ألف بينهم }

rows.speaker: الفراء وابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: A third meaning is preparing or equipping Quraysh's two journeys so they continue without interruption; Abu Jaʿfar's unhamz reading deletes the form's hamza entirely.
rows.anchor: أن يكون الإيلاف هو التهيئة والتجهيز وهو قول الفراء وابن الأعرابي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated ilaf first states the blessing broadly, then specifies the journeys to emphasize and recall its magnitude; the first phrase may encompass Quraysh's social ties, residence, travels, and circumstances, with journeys singled out as their livelihood.
rows.anchor: أنه أطلق الإيلاف أولا ثم جعل المقيد بدلا لذلك المطلق تفخيما لأمر الإيلاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The missing conjunction signals that journey-attachment is the whole blessing; affection keeps a person close, unlike obligatory attachment by command, and motivation may seek either harm's avoidance or benefit.
rows.anchor: وفائدة ترك واو العطف التنبيه على أنه كل النعمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh are descendants of al-Nadr ibn Kinana, as the Prophet reportedly affirmed that his family would not renounce its forefather.
rows.anchor: اتفقوا على أن قريشا ولد النضر بن كنانة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One etymology derives Quraysh as a diminutive of a mighty sea creature that attacks ships; Ibn Abbas says it eats and is not eaten and prevails without being overcome, apt for Quraysh's leadership and the rule of imams from them.
rows.anchor: قال : بدابة في البحر تأكل ولا تؤكل ، تعلو ولا تعلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second etymology derives Quraysh from earning, because its people profited through trade and travel.
rows.anchor: أنه مأخوذ من القرش وهو الكسب لأنهم كانوا كاسبين بتجاراتهم

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth derives the name from gathering: Qusay gathered previously dispersed clans into the sanctuary, earning the name Mujammiʿ.
rows.anchor: قال الليث : كانوا متفرقين في غير الحرم ، فجمعهم قصي بن كلاب في الحرم

rows.speaker: الشاعر أبو كم
rows.claim: A poetic line calls Qusay Mujammiʿ because God gathered the tribes of Fihr through him.
rows.anchor: ولذلك سمي قصي مجمعا ، قال الشاعر :

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A poet says God gathered Fihr tribes through Qusay, who was called Mujammiʿ.
rows.anchor: به جمع الله القبائل من فهر

rows.speaker: ابن حرة
rows.claim: A fourth etymology says Quraysh met needy pilgrims’ needs, from qarsh meaning inspection; Ibn Hurra’s verse uses al-muqarrish for a fault-finder who mocks them.
rows.anchor: ورابعها : أنهم كانوا يسدون خلة محاويج الحاج ، فسموا بذلك قريشا ، لأن القرش التفتيش قال ابن حرة :

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth defines rihla as the departure or setting out for a journey.
rows.anchor: المسألة الأولى : قال الليث : الرحلة اسم الارتحال من القول للمسير

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The common interpretation is Quraysh's winter trade journey to warmer Yemen and summer journey to Syria; Razi recounts that Hāshim organized the journeys during famine, arranging for rich merchants to share profits so poor and wealthy alike prospered.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون : كانت لقريش رحلتان رحلة بالشتاء إلى اليمن لأن اليمن أدفأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The journeys were a blessing because a successful Elephant campaign would have ended other peoples' respect for Quraysh and scattered them; their shared tribal settlement was itself a benefit, and travel especially requires affection and noble manners.
rows.anchor: أنه لو تم لأصحاب الفيل ما أرادوا ، لترك أهل الأقطار تعظيمهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second interpretation identifies the journeys as people coming to Mecca for the Rajab lesser pilgrimage in winter and the Dhu al-Hijja pilgrimage in summer, the two seasons that brought its markets and benefits; Elephant victory would have stopped them.
rows.anchor: القول الثاني : أن المراد ، رحلة الناس إلى أهل مكة فرحلة الشتاء والصيف عمرة رجب وحج ذي الحجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative rihlata is the object of ilafihim; singular can denote both journeys to avoid ambiguity, or may expand as 'the winter journey and summer journey.'
rows.anchor: المسألة الثانية : نصب الرحل بلإيلافهم مفعولا به ، وأراد رحلتي الشتاء والصيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading with ḍamma on the rāʾ, rihlah, means direction or destination.
rows.anchor: وقرىء رحلة بضم الراء وهي الجهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Blessings consist in averting harm and bringing benefit; warding harm is prior and more important, so the Elephant surah presents protection while this surah presents provision, and each should prompt worshipful gratitude.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى : { فليعبدوا رب هاذا البيت } اعلم أن الإنعام على قسمين أحدهما : دفع الضرر والثاني : جلب النفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take worship specifically as monotheism, since God rather than idols protected the House and tawhid is the key to worship; others mean bodily acts, while Razi prefers every form of worship absent contrary evidence.
rows.anchor: والأولى حمله على الكل لأن اللفظ متناول للكل إلا ما أخرجه الدليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading of 'let them worship' is that Quraysh should give up the seasonal journeys and devote themselves to the Lord who feeds them from hunger and makes them secure from fear.
rows.anchor: أن يكون معنى فليعبدوا أي فليتركوا رحلة الشتاء والصيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Him the Lord recalls Quraysh's answer to Abraha that the House had a Lord who would protect it; since they relied on Him, they owe Him their exclusive service.
rows.anchor: ولعل تخصيص لفظ الرب تقرير لما قالوه لأبرهة : إن للبيت ربا سيحفظه ، ولم يعولوا في ذلك على الأصنام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'This House' elevates the sanctuary through a reciprocal relation in which God may name servants as His, people may call Him their Lord, He is called Lord of the House, and the House is called His House.
rows.anchor: ( تارة ) يضيف نفسه إلى البيت وهو قوله : { فليعبدوا رب هاذا البيت } وتارة يضيف البيت إلى نفسه
